messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Nimble used to work on my system.
I recently upgraded to R 4, and also rtools40.

In the installer for rtools40 is no longer the checkbox for path, so I ran the line
writeLines('PATH="${RTOOLS40_HOME}\\usr\\bin;${PATH}"', con = "~/.Renviron")

like suggested on https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/  .

But alas Nimble doesn not work anymore
I unnstalled and installed Nimble again, after I ran the path code. No result.

I get an error if I run

compileNimble(model)

Error message
Error in inDL(x, as.logical(local), as.logical(now), ...) : unable to load shared object 'C:<0mitted piece of the part > /AppData/Local/Temp/RtmpuMPIxZ/nimble_generatedCode/dynamicRegistrations_05_04_17_27_49.dll': LoadLibrary failure: Kan opgegeven module niet vinden.

So he cannot find
dynamicRegistrations_05_04_17_27_49.dll.

In the folder are other files with similar names;
dynamicRegistrations_05_04_17_27_49.cpp
dynamicRegistrations_05_04_17_27_49.log
dynamicRegistrations_05_04_17_27_49.o

The log file is unfortunately empty.

Anyone a suggestion to get my nimble working again?

Thanks!

Martine

messages.body_plain:
Hi Martine,

We've heard a few other reports of problems with NIMBLE on Windows when using R 4.0.

We've found an incompatibility with R 4.0 on Windows in how we call out to the system to compile our generated C++ code.

We'll need to get a fix into our next release of nimble, but in the interim, could you please try the following (and let us know if it doesn't work):

1) You'll need the 'remotes' package installed.

2) In R, please run the following two lines of code to install a revised version of NIMBLE from a branch on our Github repository:

Sys.setenv(R_REMOTES_NO_ERRORS_FROM_WARNINGS="true")
remotes::install_github('nimble-dev/nimble','fix-win-r40', 'packages/nimble')

You'll see a bunch of messages/warnings related to our use of the Eigen package for linear algebra. You can ignore these.

Then load nimble and try the code you were having problems with.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
I would do something like this:

code <- nimbleCode({
    beta0 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    beta1 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    beta2 ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    sigma ~ dunif(0, 100)        # prior for variance components based on Gelman (2006)
    for(i in 1:n) {

        ##y[i] ~ dnorm(beta0 + beta1*x1[i] + beta2*x2[i], sd = sigma) # manual entry of linear predictors
        y[i] ~ dt(beta0 + beta1*x1[i] + beta2*x2[i], sigma, df = 3) # manual entry of linear predictors
    }
})

Note that the canonical parameterization (default parameter ordering) for the t-distribution is (mu, sigma, df), so the first argument to dt() will be the mean, the second will be sigma (standard deviation), and the third will be the degrees of freedom (df).

In my example above I hard-coded degrees of freedom as df = 3.  You could also provide a fixed value of df via the constants list, or via the initial values list if you might want to change it, or letting df itself be a model parameter and thus assigning an appropriate prior distribution to the df parameter.

Hope this helps,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am trying to use nimble to implement a logistic model with CAR model. I follow the example in the manual. The adjacent matrix I considered is based on a regular grid. When I set the grid as 4\times4, the model can be compiled, however, when the grid is larger, there is an error about nimEigen() in dcar_proper. Since I simulated the data from a car model, I think the model should work.

I downloaded the source files and found that when the size is larger, the function calculating the eigenvalues CAR_calcEVs3 will produce complex eigenvalues. Hi Simone,

Others might be able to make some suggestions of samplers and blocking to use. I haven't taken the time to think carefully about your model structure, but I'll comment on the fact that you are getting an effective sample size of 0 for mean.phi and mu.rho. This suggests that no proposals for these parameters are being accepted.

1) We often see such results when there are bad initial values for the MCMC. In particular, if the initial values are inconsistent with the model structure or each other. A simple example would be starting an MCMC with a variance component equal to 0.

2) You might try what is called a centered parameterization:

logit.phi[t] ~ dnorm(mu.phi, tau.phi)

and similarly for mu.rho.  Often non-centered parameterization such as you have now where you add mu.phi and eps.phi.

3) If you check that initial values are ok and centering doesn't help, a next diagnosis step would be to try modifying the RW samplers for mean.phi and mu.rho to have much smaller initial proposal scales. As the scale decreases, the parameters should at least mix a little bit, though each step will be small.  You can do this by using something like "control = list(scale = 0.01)" in your addSampler().

4) Some side notes:

a) You are using prod() in your model, which can lead to numerical problems compared to using sum() on the log scale. In your case it may not be possible to work on the log scale for that part of the model, but it is possible use of prod() may cause problems.

b) In nimble, one doesn't really need the zeros trick. Instead one would generally write a user-defined distribution. But if it's working as is, it's fine.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk,

The rules for a sampler are that it can expect upon entry to have the model in a fully calculated state (so, for example, model$getLogProb(nodes) can be used reliably, since this pulls cached values of log probs without calculating them) and to have the mvSaved and the model be fully in sync (all values matching).  That means that for a sampler to work correctly in the system (assuming it might be used amid other samplers in the MCMC configuration), it must ensure those two conditions are met again before it exits, for the benefit of the next sampler.

Specifically, if you have a sampler that changes the value of model[[target]], it is the sampler's responsibility to ensure those conditions upon exit.  The typical way to do so is
In setup code:
calcNodes <- model$getDependencies(target)
In run code:
model$calculate( calcNodes ) ## preferred syntax.  Usually model$getDependencies(target) is created in the setup function.
nimCopy(from = model, to = mvSaved, rowTo = 1, nodes = calcNodes, logProb = TRUE)

Of course, it would be possible to set up multiple samplers that violate the system's rules if they work in concert and you are clear what you are doing, but otherwise it is highly recommended to follow the system.

Let us know further questions.

-Perry

Hi,

I'm working on a hurdle-negative binomial model. I've specified a custom distribution that combines the hurdle with the zero-truncated negative binomial so I wouldn't need to worry about control flow related to whether the data observation was a 0 or not, and to make simulation of new data easier.

The code for the distribution is appended below. I noticed that when adding data simulation to the sampler (for the purpose of posterior predictive checks) the sampler is slowed by orders of magnitude. Is there anything obvious in the code below that could be causing this slow down?

Thanks much,
Vincent

### The distribution
dhurdlenbinom <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(x = integer(),
                 p = double(),
                 size = double(),
                 hurdle_prob = double(),
                 log = logical(0, default = 0)) {
    returnType(double())

    ## First handle zero data
    if(x == 0) {
      if(log) {## return the log probability if log = TRUE
        return(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = hurdle_prob, log = TRUE))
      } else { ## or the probability if log = FALSE
        return(dbinom(x, size = 1, prob = hurdle_prob, log = FALSE))
      }
    }

    ## If x is non-zero, use truncated nbinom
    nbinom_dens <- dnbinom(x, size = size, prob = p)
    nbinom_nonzero_prob <- 1 - dnbinom(0, size = size, prob = p)

    final_dens <- nbinom_dens / nbinom_nonzero_prob

    if(log) return(log(final_dens))
    return(final_dens)
  })
rhurdlenbinom <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(n = integer(),
                 p = double(),
                 size = double(),
                 hurdle_prob = double()) {
    returnType(integer())
    is_zero <- rbinom(1, size = 1, prob = hurdle_prob)

    if(is_zero) return(0)

    nbinom_zero_prob <- dnbinom(0, size = size, prob = p)

    x <- qnbinom(p = runif(1, nbinom_zero_prob, 1), size = size, prob = p)

    return(x)
  }
)
registerDistributions(list(
  dhurdlenbinom = list(
    BUGSdist = "dhurdlenbinom(p, size, hurdle_prob)",
    discrete = TRUE,
    range = c(0, Inf),
    types = c('value = integer()',
              'p = double()',
              'size = double()',
              'hurdle_prob = double()')
    )))

### The model code
model <- nimbleCode({
  # Likelihood
  for (i in 1:N) {
    # negative binomial mean
    mu[i] <-  (exp(X[i, 1:n_beta] %*% beta[1:n_beta]))[1, 1] # [1, 1] is hack to
                                                             # coerce to scalar

    # Moment matching to negative binomial
    p[i] <- r / (r + mu[i])

    # Hurdle probability
    hurdle_prob[i] <- (ilogit(X_hurdle[i, 1:n_beta_hurdle] %*%
                              beta_hurdle[1:n_beta_hurdle]))[1, 1]

    # Use a custom distribution so that control flow works depending on the
    # value of y
    y[i] ~ dhurdlenbinom(p = p[i], size = r, hurdle_prob = hurdle_prob[i])

    ## Simulate new data
    y_new[i] ~ dhurdlenbinom(p = p[i], size = r, hurdle_prob = hurdle_prob[i])

  }

  ## Priors
  beta_hurdle[1:n_beta_hurdle] ~ dmnorm(beta_hurdle_mu[1:n_beta_hurdle],
                                        cov = beta_hurdle_cov[1:n_beta_hurdle,
                                                              1:n_beta_hurdle])
  beta[1:n_beta] ~ dmnorm(beta_mu[1:n_beta],
                          cov = beta_cov[1:n_beta, 1:n_beta])

  r ~ dgamma(0.0001, 0.0001)

  ## Posterior predictive checks
  ynew_mean <- mean(y_new[1:N])
  p_mean <- step(ynew_mean - y_mean) # pp check for mean

  ynew_var <- var(y_new[1:N])
  p_var <- step(ynew_var - y_var) # pp check for variances

})

Thanks for the question and glad you worked it out satisfactorily on your own.

In many cases a good option for posterior predictive simulations is to do them after the MCMC has run.  You can do so with a nimbleFunction that iterates over the sample, uses copy() and/or values()<- to put values in the model, simulates from the model as needed, and extracts the simulated values.  An exception is if the posterior predictive values of interest depend on parameters or latent states that are not being monitored for the MCMC output.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Dirk,

Yes, we've run into this kind of need as well.  I can suggest two ways to do this.

First, you can make a single vector of all dependencies and then vectors of which indices are needed in which case.

Then your run code would have something like
for(j in 1:numDeps[i]) {
   logProb <- logProb + model$calculate(calcNodes[ depIndices[i, j])
}

In this case, you would be iterating over each dependency yourself

Second, and more generally, you can make a nimbleFunctionList of nimbleFunction objects (you would need a nimbleFunction for this purpose with a nimbleFunctionVirtual to serve as a base class) that manage each set of dependencies you need.  You can look up nimbleFunctionList in the User Manual and see examples in nimble's source code.

The your run code would have something like

myCalculators[[i]]$run()

for the i-th set of dependencies you need.

-Perry

Hi Dirk,

Compilation support for subsetting node vectors in model$calculate is very limited.  You will have to do something like

logProb <- 0
for(i in start_depend[zt]:end_depend[zt]) {
  logProb <- logProb + model$calculate(nodes[i])
}

Of course if you don't need the logProb sum you can omit it.

Perry
